title: Mini-Project 01 - What We Watched: Exploring Netflix Viewing Data
text:
Data Acquisition and Preparation


Code
#' Acquire Netflix What We Watched Reports
#' 
#' This function will acquire and standardize all data for MP#01
#' from Netflix. Because Netflix hosts the data files behind a CDN, we
#' are accessing the release pages and automatically extracting links to the
#' relevant files (with CDN hash). 
#' 
#' After import, files are stacked vertically and some basic cleaning is
#' performed. 
load_netflix_data <- function(){
  # Note to students: Make sure you have installed the tidyverse and fs packages
  #                   before beginning this assignment. If you aren't sure,
  #                   simply run `library(tidyverse)` at your R Console and, if
  #                   you don't see an error message, `tidyverse` has been 
  #                   installed. (Same for `fs`) If you still need to install
  #                   either package, use the `install.packages` function as 
  #                   demonstrated in class.
  library(tidyverse)
  library(rvest)
  library(readxl)
  library(fs)
  
  data_dir <- path("data", "mp01")
  
  if(!dir_exists(data_dir)){
    dir_create(data_dir, showWarnings=FALSE, recurse=TRUE)
  }
  
  NETFLIX_URLS <- list(
    `2023H1` = "https://about.netflix.com/news/what-we-watched-a-netflix-engagement-report",
    `2023H2` = "https://about.netflix.com/news/what-we-watched-the-second-half-of-2023",
    `2024H1` = "https://about.netflix.com/news/what-we-watched-the-first-half-of-2024",
    `2024H2` = "https://about.netflix.com/news/what-we-watched-the-second-half-of-2024",
    `2025H1` = "https://about.netflix.com/news/what-we-watched-the-first-half-of-2025",
    `2025H2` = "https://about.netflix.com/news/what-we-watched-the-second-half-of-2025",
    `2026H1` = "https://about.netflix.com/news/what-we-watched-the-first-half-of-2026"
  )
  
  download_if_needed <- function(url, local){
    if(!file_exists(local)){
      download.file(url, local, quiet = TRUE, mode = "wb")
    }
    
    return(local)
  }
  
  NETFLIX_URLS |> 
    map(read_html) |> 
    map(html_element, xpath = "//a[contains(@href, '.xlsx')]") |> 
    map_chr(html_attr, "href") |> 
    enframe("period", "url") |> 
    mutate(path = path(data_dir, paste0(period, ".xlsx")), 
           path = map2(url, path, download_if_needed), 
           data = map(path, read_excel, skip=3, na="*"), 
           data = map(data, \(x) x |> mutate(`Release Date` = as.Date(`Release Date`)))) |>
    unnest(data) |> 
    select(-url, -path) |> 
    mutate(year=str_sub(period, 1, 4), 
           half=str_sub(period, start=6), 
           period_start = make_date(year, if_else(half==1, 1, 7), 1), 
           period_end = make_date(year, if_else(half==1, 6, 12), if_else(half==1, 30, 31))) |> 
    filter(!is.na(`Hours Viewed`)) |> 
    mutate(live_event = !is.na(Runtime) & str_detect(Runtime, "\\d+:\\d+\\*"), 
           clean_time = str_remove(Runtime, fixed("*")),
           Runtime = 60 * hour(hm(clean_time)) + minute(hm(clean_time))) |>
    select(-clean_time) |>
    mutate(Runtime = coalesce(Runtime, mean(Runtime, na.rm=TRUE)), 
           .by=Title, 
           Title = stringi::stri_trans_general(Title, "Latin-ASCII"),
           Title = str_remove(Title, " // .*"), 
           Title = str_remove(Title, "[^[:ascii:]].*"), 
           Title = str_trim(Title)) |>
    filter_out(Title == "") |>
    select(year, 
           period, 
           period_start, 
           period_end, 
           Title, 
           -half, 
           Runtime, 
           Views, 
           `Hours Viewed`, 
           `Release Date`,
           `Available Globally?`, 
           live_event) |>
    rename(title = Title, runtime = Runtime, views = Views,
           hours_viewed = `Hours Viewed`, release = `Release Date`,
           avail_global = `Available Globally?`) |>
    mutate(year = as.integer(year), avail_global = avail_global == "Yes")
}

text:
Exploratory Data Analysis
Initial EDA pass to check data types, make sure all changes made to code function as intended, and take a look at basic statistics to see if anything stands out. First impression: there are quite a few data points missing from “runtime”, “release”, and “views”, which will hinder my ability to get a full picture of Netflix’s true performance. However, if we simply remove these missing values from the working data set, we can at least see what the behavior is like above a minimum value for these variables. One statistic that stands out to me is the median runtime (320 minutes) versus the mean (467.35 minutes). I would be curious to know if that difference is significant and, if it is, what skewed runtimes would mean in terms of views.

List of all the titles with viewership at least one standard deviation above the mean in every period.



Code
# 1. Determine the total number of periods available in the data
total_periods <- n_distinct(NETFLIX_DATA$period)

# 2. Identify titles that are 1 SD above the mean in EVERY period
highly_viewed_staples <- NETFLIX_DATA |> 
  group_by(period) |> 
  mutate(
    # Calculate the threshold for 1 Standard Deviation above the Mean for each specific period
    sd_threshold = mean(hours_viewed, na.rm = TRUE) + sd(hours_viewed, na.rm = TRUE)
  ) |> 
  # Keep only the rows where a show beat its period's threshold
  filter(hours_viewed >= sd_threshold) |> 
  ungroup() |> 
  
  # Group by title to see how consistently they achieved this across periods
  group_by(title) |> 
  summarise(
    periods_above_threshold = n_distinct(period),
    overall_avg_hours       = mean(hours_viewed, na.rm = TRUE),
    overall_min_hours       = min(hours_viewed, na.rm = TRUE),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) |> 
  # CRITICAL FILTER: The title must have met the condition in ALL periods
  filter(periods_above_threshold == total_periods) |> 
  arrange(desc(overall_min_hours))

# 3. Render into a clean summary table
highly_viewed_staples |> 
  select(title, overall_avg_hours, overall_min_hours) |> 
  gt() |> 
  tab_header(
    title = "Netflix Elite Staples",
    subtitle = "Titles with viewership at least 1 standard deviation above the mean in every reporting period"
  ) |> 
  cols_label(
    title = "Show Title",
    overall_avg_hours = "Average Hours / Period",
    overall_min_hours = "Lowest Period (Minimum Hours)"
  ) |> 
  fmt_integer(
    columns = c(overall_avg_hours, overall_min_hours)
  ) |> 
  tab_options(
    heading.title.font.weight = "bold"
  )

Viewership breakdown per period, movies versus shows. I omitted all titles whose runtimes were not available and defined a movie title as any with a runtime under four hours. Viewers clearly spend more time watching shows versus movies at roughly .



Code
# 1. Filter out missing runtimes, classify, and compute viewership share
format_share_table_clean <- NETFLIX_DATA |> 
  # CRITICAL FIX: Drops rows where runtime is missing (NA)
  filter(!is.na(runtime)) |> 
  mutate(
    # Classify everything strictly less than 240 mins as Movie, else Show
    content_type = if_else(runtime < 240, "Movie", "Show")
  ) |> 
  group_by(period, content_type) |> 
  summarise(
    type_hours = sum(hours_viewed, na.rm = TRUE),
    .groups = "drop_last" # Leaves group by period active for the division step
  ) |> 
  mutate(
    # Calculate fraction of time spent on this category within the specific period
    time_fraction = type_hours / sum(type_hours)
  ) |> 
  ungroup()

# 2. Pivot the data wider for a side-by-side layout
format_share_table_clean |> 
  select(period, content_type, time_fraction) |> 
  pivot_wider(
    names_from = content_type, 
    values_from = time_fraction
  ) |> 
  # 3. Render beautifully with gt
  gt() |> 
  tab_header(
    title = "Viewership Share: Shows vs. Movies (Cleaned Data)",
    subtitle = "Excludes titles with missing runtimes. Movies defined as titles under 240 minutes."
  ) |> 
  cols_label(
    period = "Period",
    Movie = "Movies Share",
    Show = "Shows Share"
  ) |> 
  fmt_percent(
    columns = c(Movie, Show),
    decimals = 1
  ) |> 
  tab_options(
    heading.title.font.weight = "bold"
  )

General viewership and the viewership of the top 1% for live events versus recorded content. Given the vastly smaller number of live events (roughly 20x less total titles), the resulting viewership is about equal in general and a little less than half in the top 1%. This result signals a potential opportunity for Netflix to shift focus in 2027.



Code
# 1. Compute Average and 'Top Tier' metrics using views instead of hours
live_vs_pre_views <- NETFLIX_DATA |> 
  group_by(live_event) |> 
  summarise(
    # Count of entries in this category
    total_titles = n_distinct(title),
    
    # Standard Average (Mean) Views
    mean_views   = mean(views, na.rm = TRUE),
    
    # 'Top Tier' Performance (99th percentile of views)
    top_tier_views = quantile(views, probs = 0.99, na.rm = TRUE),
    
    .groups = "drop"
  ) |> 
  # Clean up labels for the final display
  mutate(content_format = if_else(live_event == TRUE, "Live Event", "Pre-Taped Content"))

# 2. Render beautifully with gt
live_vs_pre_views |> 
  select(content_format, total_titles, mean_views, top_tier_views) |> 
  gt() |> 
  tab_header(
    title = "Performance Analysis: Live Events vs. Pre-Taped Content",
    subtitle = "Comparing typical performance and elite top-tier boundaries using standardized Views"
  ) |> 
  cols_label(
    content_format = "Content Format",

title: Mini-Project 01 - What We Watched: Exploring Netflix Viewing Data
text:
Final Insights and Deliverable
Platform Strategy Memo
From my analysis, there are some clear opportunities for growth in 2027, if Netflix commits budgetary power to a couple of key areas. The first area of potential interest is increasing offerings of live events. Considering the weight of average views per live event is about 13.4% higher than that of recorded content, focusing on licensing or hosting more live events would undoubtedly have a positive impact on subscriptions. The cost could be mitigated by mixing in low- and mid-tier sports offerings. One major advantage of top-tier live events is the potential for paid content. Pay-per-views would be an attractive opportunity to capture additional revenue for top-tier live events. Finally, adding live news and politics may also attract more people among older demographics, thereby increasing the variety of the Netflix subscriber base.
Another area of potential interest is increasing globally available content. According to the data, globally available content accounts for 52% of the hours viewed yet only 35% of Netflix’s titles are globally available. This could be remedied by expanding the reach of existing catalog content, adding more subtitled/dubbed features, and creating new, more culturally versatile content. Also, partnerships with international studios (as in the case of Squid Games) would allow Netflix to produce original content at significantly lower cost, thereby increasing the viewership gain per value cost.
The last area of potential is in the consistent gap between hours spent watching movies versus watching shows. The ratio of hours spent watching shows versus movies is roughly 9-to1, yet the cost of producing a movie versus a show is significantly higher per hour of content. This means the viewership gain per value cost is much lower for movies than it is for shows. My recommendation is for Netflix to start producing more theatrical releases alongside their usual platform releases. This would allow Netflix an opportunity to capture more revenue at lower cost, considering advertising on their own platform would greatly reduce marketing overhead. It would also allow Netflix to attract potential subscribers both domestically and globally.
Although Netflix is a powerhouse and leader in the streaming sector, there are still avenues for improvement and optimization. By increasing the number of live events per year, reworking the existing catalog to include more cultural diversity, and producing more theatrical movie releases, Netflix can realize much higher earning potential in 2027.
